1233.title: The coiled one remains
1233.hook: what if four children were killed; the coiled serpent still lives, he writes (Zafarnama)
1233.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the four Sahibzade in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their martyrdom; the Zafarnama's line about the coiled serpent is often recited in katha and at those gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, broken oaths: an emperor held to the promises he made in God's name. Your line was keep your oath.

Some sentences are short because nothing more could be said. The Zafarnama has one of those. Sikh tradition remembers what came before the letter: the Guru's four sons were killed. Two, tradition says, fell fighting. Two, still small boys, were put to death because they would not give up their faith. You heard their story on days eighty-nine and ninety. A father who had lost all four children wrote to the emperor, and the line he wrote about it is not a lament. It's a question, followed by an image Sikhs still repeat.
screen: `A SHORT SENTENCE.` → `FOUR SONS LOST.` → `A QUESTION, THEN AN IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the line runs like this: what of it, if you have killed four children? The coiled serpent still remains. The first half names the worst thing that could happen to a parent, and names it flatly, almost as a shrug. That flatness is not coldness. It's refusal. He will not let the loss be the end of the sentence. The second half turns to the coiled one. A coiled snake is a snake at rest and fully alive, gathered into itself, not beaten. Readers hear different things in it. Some hear the Guru speaking of himself: you took my sons, and I am still here. Some hear the Khalsa, the community he had formed: you can kill children, and you have not killed the people. Some hear both, and a warning folded inside: a coiled thing can still rise. Whichever reading, the line is about what remains after the loss, not about the loss itself. And stay with what it doesn't say. It doesn't say the grief is small. Sikhs remember the four sons, the Sahibzade, with deep sorrow, in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their deaths. The coiled one remains is not a way of skipping the mourning. It's what stands up in the middle of it.

segments.voice: If it feels right, bring to mind a loss you've carried and let it be as heavy as it is; then, gently, look for what is still standing in you: a habit you kept, someone you still look after, a way you still laugh. If you pray, hold both the loss and what remains in Waheguru. If a loss ever feels heavier than you can carry, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

Your line: still standing. Coiled and quiet is not the same as beaten. See you tomorrow.

1234.title: Trust in protection
1234.hook: he writes that no one can harm the one the Lord protects (Zafarnama)
1234.howItsDone: Sikhs recite prayers for protection in the evening, and the Zafarnama's lines on the Lord as protector are recalled in katha as a picture of trust that stands alongside action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coiled one remains: four sons lost, and still something stands. Your line was still standing.

Who gets to say the word safe? A child in a warm house says it easily. A man who, tradition says, has lost his home and his four sons has every reason never to say it again. And yet in the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes confident lines about exactly that: being protected. He writes them to the emperor himself, whose armies had chased him. Not a promise of safety from someone who has never been hurt, but from someone who has.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SAY SAFE?` → `WRITTEN AFTER EVERYTHING WAS LOST.` → `SENT TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the thought runs like this: what can an enemy do, when the Friend is kind? The One who protects is the Lord, and no one can harm the one the Lord protects. In the letter, the Friend is God. It can't mean nothing bad will ever happen. The man writing it has already lived through the worst. So protected must mean something else. Some readers hear it this way: what the emperor can reach is the body, the fort, the family's lives. What he cannot reach is the bond between the Guru and God, and the faith that made the Khalsa. That's what is held, and that's what no army can take. The trust doesn't make him passive, either. The same letter argues, accuses, and keeps going. Trust in protection, in the Guru's life, sits right alongside action. It's the floor he stands on while he works, not a reason to stop working. And there's a turn in who he's speaking to. Telling the emperor, in effect, you cannot harm me is not a boast about armies. It's a statement about where real power lies. For the Guru, it lies with the Friend. Sikh prayer, too, asks Waheguru for protection. Read beside this letter, that prayer isn't asking for a life without loss. It's asking to be held through it.
screen: `WHAT CAN AN ENEMY DO?` · `NOT: NOTHING BAD WILL HAPPEN.` · `TRUST SITS RIGHT BESIDE ACTION.` · `WHERE REAL POWER LIES.` · then, large: `PROTECTED.`

1235.title: The ten shabads
1235.hook: ten hymns of longing, including the song from the wilderness
1235.howItsDone: Sikhs sing the Shabad Hazare of Guru Gobind Singh in kirtan, and Mittar pyare nu is often sung slowly in gurdwaras and at gatherings remembering the Guru's time in the Machhiwara forest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trust in protection: no enemy can harm the one the Lord protects, written by a man who had lost nearly everything. Your line was protected.

Night, in a forest. Tradition places Guru Gobind Singh there after the battle at Chamkaur, which you met on day eighty-nine, alone or nearly so, sleeping on the ground with a stone or a clod of earth for a pillow. A general would plan. A father would weep. Tradition says he sang. And what he sang wasn't a battle song or a lament. It was a love song, addressed to a Friend. It is collected with other hymns of his under one name, and that name is today's word.
screen: `NIGHT, IN A FOREST.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `HE SANG A LOVE SONG.`

segments.voice: Shabad Hazare is the name of a small group of hymns by Guru Gobind Singh, ten of them, set to ragas so they can be sung. They are short, and they share a mood: longing for God, and impatience with anything that pretends to be devotion without the heart in it. One of them, paraphrased, tells the mind how to be a true renunciate: treat your own home as the forest, stay detached inside while you live in the world. No need to run off; take the forest with you. Among the ten is the wilderness song, Mittar pyare nu, haal mureedan da kehna. Tell the beloved Friend how his disciples are faring. Then, paraphrased, the song lists the comforts of home and turns every one of them sour. Without you, a soft quilt is like a sickness. Living in fine houses is like living with snakes. The cup and the flask are like blades. And then the turn: the Friend's bare straw bed is better than a comfortable life in burning mansions. The man who has lost everything is not mourning the comforts. He is saying they were never the point. The ground is fine, if the Friend is near. Sikhs sing this song in kirtan, sometimes very slowly. Ten hymns, then, but one thread through all of them: what matters is nearness to the Beloved, wherever you happen to sleep.

segments.voice: If you can, let a recording of Mittar pyare nu, or any of the Shabad Hazare, play, and listen to the shape of the longing more than the words. If not, sit with the image, the straw bed, the open sky and a Friend nearby, and notice what you'd keep if the comforts went. If you pray, let the name Waheguru ride under the music.

1236.title: By their grace I won
1236.hook: in praise of his Sikhs he writes that by their grace he won battles and gave gifts (Khalsa Mahima)
1236.howItsDone: Sikhs recite and sing the Khalsa Mahima swayyas of Guru Gobind Singh, especially at gatherings about the Khalsa, and its refrain is often recalled when speaking of the respect owed to the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shabad Hazare: a love song from the wilderness, and a straw bed better than mansions. Your line was ten hymns.

Three words, said again and again, like a drumbeat. Inhi ke prasad. They close one phrase and open the next, so the poem never gets far from them. The poet is Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru his Sikhs followed. The poem is known as Khalsa Mahima, the praise of the Khalsa. And the three words point not upward to him, but outward, at the people who followed him: everything I have, I have through you.
screen: `CREDIT USUALLY FLOWS UP.` → `KHALSA MAHIMA.` → `EVERYTHING I HAVE, THROUGH YOU.`

segments.voice: The poem's lines are built on one repeated phrase: inhi ke prasad. By their grace. Paraphrased, it runs: by their grace I won battles. By their grace I gave gifts. By their grace my troubles were cut away, and by their grace my house is full. Otherwise, he says, there are countless poor ones like me. Prasad is the same word Sikhs know from the Mool Mantar's closing, gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. Normally grace comes from the Guru to the Sikh. Here the Guru turns it around and says grace has come from the Sikhs to him. That's not false modesty. Tradition sets the poem at a moment when someone questioned why the Guru gave so generously to his Sikhs, and this is his answer: they are worth it, because what I am, they made. It fits the Khalsa he formed. Tradition remembers that after he initiated the first Khalsa, he asked them to initiate him in turn. The teacher stood in line behind his students. Khalsa Mahima puts that same picture into verse. Look at what he lists: not only victories. Gifts. A full house. The ordinary goods of a life. He traces them to people, not to his own skill. For Sikhs, the line sits underneath a habit visible in gurdwaras: the sangat, the community, is treated with deep respect, and this poem is one reason Sikhs give.

1237.title: Chandi di Var
1237.hook: a Punjabi ballad of the goddess's battle; its first stanza gives the Ardas its opening; Sikhs read its imagery as divine power
1237.howItsDone: Sikhs stand with folded hands for the Ardas at the close of services and before important moments, and its opening lines come from the first stanza of Chandi di Var: first remember Bhagauti, then Guru Nanak and the Gurus after him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khalsa Mahima: the Guru saying he won, gave and lived by his Sikhs' grace. Your line was by their grace.

Stand in a gurdwara at the end of a service. Everyone rises. Hands are folded. One person leads the Ardas, the standing prayer you met on day five, and its first words are ones Sikhs say at weddings and at funerals, in good times and hard ones: Prithm Bhagauti simar kai. First, remember Bhagauti. Then Guru Nanak. Those words are not from the Guru Granth Sahib. They come from a less expected place: the opening of a war ballad, in Punjabi, by Guru Gobind Singh. Today, that ballad.
screen: `EVERYONE RISES FOR ARDAS.` → `FIRST, REMEMBER BHAGAUTI.` → `FROM A WAR BALLAD.`

segments.voice: Chandi di Var means the ballad of Chandi. A var is a Punjabi ballad, a form for heroes and battles, meant to be sung with drive. Chandi is a name of the goddess known in Hindu stories as Durga, and the ballad tells her battle against demons who had driven the gods from their place. The verses are full of clashing steel, drums and the dust of the field. Then there is the opening stanza. Paraphrased: first remember Bhagauti, then meditate on Guru Nanak, then Angad, Amar Das and Ram Das, then Arjan, Har Gobind and Har Rai, then Har Krishan, whose sight takes away all suffering, then Tegh Bahadur. May they help us everywhere. Those are the lines Sikhs say, standing, at the start of the Ardas, with more added after them. How do Sikhs read a ballad about a goddess? Sikhs read Bhagauti here as divine power, God's power, and some hear it as the sword, the power that protects the weak. The goddess's battle becomes a picture of that power at work against injustice. As this block began by saying, Sikhs discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth come from the Guru's own pen. Whatever view a Sikh holds, this stanza lives in the Ardas, said standing. Before naming a single Guru, it remembers the power behind them all. Then it lists the Gurus one by one, like a family calling its ancestors by name.

1238.title: The thirty-three swayyas
1238.hook: verses on true devotion and against empty ritual
1238.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the first of Guru Gobind Singh's thirty-three swayyas when teaching what it means to be Khalsa, and the set is read in katha as a call to inner devotion over outward show.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chandi di Var: a war ballad whose first stanza opens the Ardas, with the power remembered first. Your line was the power remembered.

A uniform tells you what someone is supposed to be. It doesn't tell you what they are. A white coat, a badge, a robe, a turban, a cross on a chain: each one makes a promise on the outside. Traditions have had to ask what happens when the outside and the inside don't match. Guru Gobind Singh asks it in a set of verses in a form called the swayya. There are thirty-three of them, and they keep circling one question: what does real devotion look like, under the clothes?
screen: `A UNIFORM MAKES A PROMISE.` → `OUTSIDE AND INSIDE.` → `THIRTY-THREE SWAYYAS.`

segments.voice: A swayya is a verse form, a stanza with a strong, rolling beat, good for reciting aloud. The thirty-three swayyas sit among Guru Gobind Singh's writings, and the first one says who is Khalsa. Paraphrased: the one who remembers, day and night, the light that never goes out; who brings no one but the One into the mind; who is full of love and trust; who does not, even by mistake, put faith in fasts, tombs, shrines and outward rites; who knows the One beyond pilgrimage, charity, austerity and self-control. When that perfect light shines in the heart, know that one as Khalsa, pure. The light comes first. The love and trust come next. The outward things are not mocked for fun; they're simply moved out of the center. Pilgrimage and charity aren't called evil. They're called not enough, on their own, without the One. Other swayyas in the set are sharper. They turn on people who wear religious dress to impress, or to collect money from the faithful, while their hearts are elsewhere. That edge isn't aimed at one community. It's aimed at a habit any community can fall into, Sikhs included, and some Sikh teachers read it that way: as a mirror for their own house first. The verses ask a hard, simple thing. Not, what do you wear, or where have you traveled, but is the light awake inside?
screen: `A SWAYYA: A ROLLING VERSE.` · `THE LIGHT THAT NEVER GOES OUT.` · `NOT EVIL, JUST NOT ENOUGH.` · `A MIRROR FOR YOUR OWN HOUSE.` · then, large: `TRUE DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: Read the first of the thirty-three slowly, once, in any language, or take the paraphrase you just heard. Then ask, gently, which of your habits are outside and which are inside, without judging either list, and rest your attention on the breath as if it were a small light that doesn't go out. 1239.title: Names of weapons
1239.hook: a long poem of weapon-names used as names of the Divine
1239.howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan as one of the articles of faith, and Sikh teachers explain it, and the weapon names of Shastar Nam Mala, as signs of God's power used to protect the weak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirty-three swayyas: devotion under the clothes, the light awake inside. Your line was true devotion.

Sword. Dagger. Arrow. Axe. Musket. Say them in a row and they sound like an inventory, or a threat. Now say them in a row as names for God. That's what one poem among Guru Gobind Singh's writings does. It's called Shastar Nam Mala, the garland of weapon names, and it reads like a rosary strung with blades. For some listeners that's jarring, even unsettling. For Sikhs it is a way of seeing, and today is about what that way sees.
screen: `SWORD, DAGGER, ARROW, AXE.` → `NAMES FOR GOD?` → `A GARLAND OF WEAPON NAMES.`

segments.voice: Shastar means weapon, nam means name, and a mala is a garland, the same word used for a string of prayer beads. The poem opens, paraphrased, by listing weapons, sword, kirpan, khanda, musket, axe and arrow, and calling them our pir, our guides. Then it moves through name after name of weapons, and through them names the Divine. Why pray like that? Sikhs answer in a few connected ways. First, a weapon here stands for power, and in Sikh teaching all power belongs to God. To name the blade is to name the One whose strength it borrows. Second, the power is for protection. Sikhs speak of the sword as the defender of the weak, the thing that stands between the bully and the person being bullied. The Zafarnama says it plainly, in paraphrase: when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first. Third, the poem trains attention. A tool takes on the purpose of the hand that holds it. The same edge that cuts bread can wound. Naming it as God's is a reminder of whose purpose it must serve. Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan, one of the five Ks from day eighteen, as an article of faith, not as an ornament and not as a threat. It's a vow worn at the hip. Looking back over this week: still standing, protected, ten hymns, by their grace, the power remembered, true devotion. Today closes it with power held in the right hands.
screen: `A GARLAND OF NAMES.` · `ALL POWER BELONGS TO GOD.` · `THE DEFENDER OF THE WEAK.` · `A TOOL IS NEVER NEUTRAL.` · then, large: `TOOLS FOR GOOD.`
